title: Book 5 — Terpsichore, Chapter 67
paragraphs: In these matters it seems to me that this Cleisthenes was imitating his mother's father, Cleisthenes the tyrant of Sicyon. For when that Cleisthenes went to war with Argos, he first put a stop in Sicyon to the contests of rhapsodes, which were concerned with the poems of Homer, because Argives and Argos are praised in them almost everywhere. Secondly, since there was (as there still is) in the very marketplace of the Sicyonians a hero-shrine of Adrastus, son of Talaus, Cleisthenes conceived a desire to cast him out of the land because he was an Argive. So he came to Delphi and consulted the oracle as to whether he should cast Adrastus out; and the Pythian priestess answered that Adrastus was king of the Sicyonians, whereas he was a stoner of them. Since the god did not permit him to do this, he went away home and considered means by which Adrastus might be brought to leave of his own accord; and when he thought he had discovered them, he sent to Thebes in Boeotia and said that he wished to introduce Melanippus, son of Astacus, into his city, and the Thebans gave him leave. So Cleisthenes introduced Melanippus into his city, appointed a sacred enclosure for him within the precincts of the city hall itself, and established him there in the strongest position. Cleisthenes introduced Melanippus (for I must report this too) because he was the greatest enemy of Adrastus, having killed both his brother Mecisteus and his son-in-law Tydeus. Once he had appointed the sacred enclosure for him, Cleisthenes took away the sacrifices and festivals of Adrastus and gave them to Melanippus. Now the Sicyonians had been accustomed to honor Adrastus with very great honors; for this land was formerly the land of Polybus, and Adrastus was the son of Polybus's daughter, and Polybus, dying without sons, gave his kingdom to Adrastus. The Sicyonians accordingly gave other honors to Adrastus, but especially, with reference to his sufferings, they honored him with tragic choruses, paying this honor not to Dionysus but to Adrastus. Cleisthenes, however, gave the choruses back to Dionysus, and the other rites besides these he gave to Melanippus.
